title: Add Two Integers Without + or -
statement: You are given two integers a and b. Each fits in a signed 32-bit range (-2^31 to 2^31 - 1), either may be negative, and their true sum is guaranteed to fit in the same signed 32-bit range. Return their sum a + b as a plain integer, but you may not use the + or - operators anywhere in your code (no addition, subtraction, unary negation, or increment tricks). Build the sum out of bitwise operations instead: XOR gives the sum of two numbers ignoring carries, and AND followed by a left shift gives the carries. Because Python integers have unlimited width, you must simulate a fixed 32-bit machine by masking intermediate values with 0xFFFFFFFF, and if the final masked result has its top bit set (value >= 0x80000000) you must convert it back to the corresponding negative Python int before returning it. The returned value must be exactly equal to a + b.
hints: If you add two binary numbers by hand, which bit operation gives you the digit sums when you ignore all carries, and which gives you just the carries?

Repeat: sum-without-carry is a ^ b, carry is (a & b) << 1; the loop ends when the carry is zero. But Python ints are infinitely wide, so a negative operand never runs out of 1-bits -- mask every intermediate value with 0xFFFFFFFF to emulate 32-bit hardware.

Start with a &= 0xFFFFFFFF and b &= 0xFFFFFFFF; loop a, b = (a ^ b) & 0xFFFFFFFF, ((a & b) << 1) & 0xFFFFFFFF while b is nonzero; finally, if a >= 0x80000000 the 32-bit result is negative, so return ~(a ^ 0xFFFFFFFF), otherwise return a.
